rows.stem: The molar ionic conductivities of \(\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}\) and \(\mathrm{Cl^-}\) are 119.0 and 76.3 \(\mathrm{S\ cm^2\ mol^{-1}}\) respectively. The value of limiting molar conductivity of \(\mathrm{CaCl_2}\) will be :
rows.solution:
By Kohlrausch's law the limiting molar conductivity is the sum of the contributions of ALL the ions the formula unit gives, each counted as often as it appears.

Calcium chloride gives ONE calcium ion and TWO chloride ions:
\(\Lambda_m^{\circ}(\mathrm{CaCl_2}) = \lambda^{\circ}_{\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}} + 2\lambda^{\circ}_{\mathrm{Cl^-}}\)
\(= 119{\cdot}0 + 2(76{\cdot}3) = 119{\cdot}0 + 152{\cdot}6\)

\(\Lambda_m^{\circ} = 271{\cdot}6\ \mathrm{S\ cm^2\ mol^{-1}}\)

The factor of 2 is the whole question. Adding the two figures once gives 195.3, which is offered as the trap — it would be the answer for a 1:1 electrolyte such as potassium chloride, not for this one.

rows.subtopic: Chemical Reactions of Aldehydes and Ketones
rows.stem:
Consider the following reaction :
\(\mathrm{H_2C=O} + \mathrm{H_2C=O} + \mathrm{Conc}{\cdot}\,\mathrm{KOH} \xrightarrow{\Delta} \mathrm{A} + \mathrm{B}\)
Identify A and B from the given options :
rows.figureNote: ILLUSTRATIVE — both reactants are printed as DRAWN structures: two identical H-above / H-below carbonyls, each 'H\C=O' with slanted bonds meeting a central C. They are written above as the condensed formula \(\mathrm{H_2C=O}\), which is the same molecule and loses nothing, and deliberately NOT named — option (C) contains the word 'Methanal', so naming the reactant in the stem would leak. The real crop should still be attached. Page idx 4.
rows.solution:
The reagents are two molecules of METHANAL with concentrated alkali, which is the CANNIZZARO reaction.

Methanal has NO \(\alpha\)-hydrogen — it has no carbon next to the carbonyl at all — so it cannot undergo aldol condensation and disproportionates instead: one molecule is REDUCED to the alcohol while another is OXIDISED to the salt of the acid.

\(2\mathrm{HCHO} + \text{conc. }\mathrm{KOH} \xrightarrow{\Delta} \mathrm{CH_3OH} + \mathrm{HCOOK}\)

\(\mathrm{A}\) is METHANOL and \(\mathrm{B}\) is POTASSIUM FORMATE.

The carbon count settles the two distractors offering ethanol or potassium acetate: each molecule of methanal has ONE carbon, and the Cannizzaro reaction does not join carbon skeletons — it only moves hydrogen between two molecules.

rows.stem: Which of the following acids represents Vitamin C ?
rows.solution:
Vitamin C is ASCORBIC ACID.

It is water soluble, so the body cannot store it and a regular dietary supply is needed; a deficiency causes scurvy, in which the gums bleed and wounds fail to heal.

The other three acids are all related to glucose chemistry or to the benzene ring, and none is a vitamin. GLUCONIC acid is what bromine water makes from glucose by oxidising the aldehyde alone; SACCHARIC acid is what concentrated nitric acid makes by oxidising both ends; BENZOIC acid is a simple aromatic acid used as a food preservative.

rows.stem: Rosenmund reduction is used for the preparation of Aldehydes. The catalyst used in this reaction is
rows.solution:
The catalyst is PALLADIUM SUPPORTED ON BARIUM SULPHATE, \(\mathrm{Pd{-}BaSO_4}\).

Rosenmund reduction converts an ACYL CHLORIDE to an ALDEHYDE, and the difficulty is stopping there — an ordinary hydrogenation catalyst would carry the reduction on to the primary alcohol.

\(\mathrm{R{-}COCl} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{BaSO_4}]{\mathrm{H_2}/\mathrm{Pd}} \mathrm{R{-}CHO} + \mathrm{HCl}\)

The barium sulphate is a POISON, deliberately added to moderate the palladium's activity, and sulphur or quinoline is often added for the same purpose. A catalyst that is too good is the problem this reaction solves.

Of the others, anhydrous aluminium chloride is the Friedel-Crafts catalyst, iron(III) oxide appears in the Haber process, and mercury(II) sulphate catalyses the hydration of alkynes.

rows.stem: Which alkyl halide from the given options will undergo \(\mathrm{S_N1}\) reaction faster ?
rows.solution:
2-BROMO-2-METHYLPROPANE, \((\mathrm{CH_3})_3\mathrm{C{-}Br}\), reacts fastest.

The rate of an \(\mathrm{S_N}1\) reaction is set entirely by how easily the CARBOCATION forms, since that is the slow step — so the question is which cation is the most stable.

This compound is TERTIARY, and its cation is stabilised by electron release from THREE methyl groups. 2-Bromopropane is secondary with two, and bromoethane primary with one.

The fourth option is the interesting one. \((\mathrm{CH_3})_3\mathrm{C{-}CH_2{-}Br}\) LOOKS crowded, but its bromine sits on a \(-\mathrm{CH_2}-\) group, so it is PRIMARY — the bulk is on the NEIGHBOURING carbon, where it hinders the bimolecular route without stabilising the cation at all.

rows.subtopic: General Properties of the Transition Elements (d-Block)
rows.stem: From the elements of 3d series given below, which element shows the maximum number of oxidation states ?
rows.solution:
MANGANESE shows the maximum number of oxidation states.

The highest state a transition metal reaches is the sum of its \(ns\) and unpaired \((n-1)d\) electrons. Manganese is \([\mathrm{Ar}]\,3d^5 4s^2\) — five unpaired d electrons plus two \(4s\) — so it can reach \(5 + 2 = 7\), and it runs the whole way from \(+2\) to \(+7\).

Chromium comes next with \(5 + 1 = 6\), titanium reaches \(+4\), and scandium has only \(+3\).

The pattern across the series is that the number of states rises to a maximum in the MIDDLE and falls away at either end — at the start there are too few d electrons to give up, and at the end they are too tightly held to be available.

rows.subtopic: Temperature Dependence of the Rate of a Reaction
rows.stem: The correct Mathematical expression of Arrhenius equation is
rows.solution:
The Arrhenius equation is
\(k = Ae^{-E_a/RT}\)

Read the form rather than remember it. The exponent must be NEGATIVE, because \(e^{-E_a/RT}\) is the FRACTION of molecules carrying at least the activation energy, and a fraction cannot exceed 1. The option with a positive exponent would give a value greater than 1 and a rate constant larger than the collision frequency, which is impossible.

The pre-exponential factor \(A\) must also be POSITIVE, since it counts collisions of the right orientation — so the two options carrying a minus sign in front of \(A\) would give a negative rate constant, and a reaction cannot proceed at a negative rate.

The option without \(A\) at all loses the collision frequency and leaves a dimensionless fraction where a rate constant belongs.

rows.stem: Identify the tertiary amine from the following :
rows.solution:
The tertiary amine is \(\mathrm{CH_3{-}N(CH_3){-}CH_3}\), trimethylamine.

An amine is classified by how many CARBON groups are attached to its NITROGEN — not by the kind of carbon the nitrogen sits on, which is the distinction this question is testing.

Trimethylamine's nitrogen carries THREE methyl groups and no hydrogen at all, so it is tertiary.

The other three all have their nitrogen attached to only ONE carbon or two. \(\mathrm{CH_3{-}NH{-}CH_2CH_3}\) has two carbons on nitrogen and is SECONDARY. Both \(\mathrm{CH_3CH(NH_2)CH_3}\) and \((\mathrm{C_2H_5})_2\mathrm{CHNH_2}\) are PRIMARY — each has a single carbon on the nitrogen — even though that carbon is itself secondary or tertiary. The classification of an ALCOHOL works the other way round, by the carbon, which is where the confusion comes from.

rows.subtopic: Chemical Reactions of Aldehydes and Ketones
rows.stem: Nucleophilic addition of Grignard reagent to ketones followed by hydrolysis with dilute acids forms :
rows.solution:
The product is a TERTIARY ALCOHOL.

A Grignard reagent adds its carbanion-like carbon to the carbonyl carbon, and hydrolysis then gives an alcohol. What CLASS of alcohol results depends on how many carbon groups the carbonyl carbon already carried.

A KETONE carries TWO carbon groups. Adding the Grignard's carbon makes THREE, so the carbinol carbon ends up attached to three carbons and no hydrogen — a tertiary alcohol:
\(\mathrm{R_2C{=}O} \xrightarrow[2.\ \mathrm{H_3O^+}]{1.\ \mathrm{R'MgX}} \mathrm{R_2C(OH)R'}\)

The pattern runs right through: METHANAL, with no carbon groups, gives a PRIMARY alcohol; any other ALDEHYDE, with one, gives a SECONDARY alcohol; a ketone gives a tertiary one. Counting the carbon groups on the carbonyl carbon predicts all three.

rows.stem: In a given graph of zero order reaction, the slope and intercept are :
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED — the stem says 'In a given graph' and names neither axis, so it is unanswerable from the text alone: the printed plot is a straight line falling from the y-intercept to the x-axis, with the y-axis labelled 'Concentration of R' and the x-axis 'Time', and the options turn entirely on what is plotted against what. The axis labels are deliberately NOT copied into the stem, since reading them off the graph is the step the question tests. Page idx 6.
rows.solution:
For a zero order reaction the slope is \(-k\) and the intercept is \([\mathrm{R}]_0\).

A zero order reaction proceeds at a constant rate, \(\text{Rate} = k\), so integrating gives
\([\mathrm{R}] = [\mathrm{R}]_0 - kt\)

Compare with \(y = c + mx\), taking \(y\) as \([\mathrm{R}]\) and \(x\) as \(t\): the intercept is the starting concentration and the slope is \(-k\).

The slope is NEGATIVE because the reactant is being consumed, so the line falls — and it falls at a steady rate all the way to zero, which is what distinguishes zero order from every other.

The two options carrying 2.303 belong to the FIRST order plot of \(\log[\mathrm{R}]\) against \(t\), and the option with a positive slope would describe a reactant whose concentration rises with time.

rows.stem:
Match the reagents required for the given reactions :
I. Oxidation of primary alcohols to aldehydes
II. Butan-2-one to Butan-2-ol
III. Bromination of Phenol to 2, 4, 6-Tribromophenol
IV. Dehydration of propan-2-ol to propene
(p) \(\mathrm{NaBH_4}\)
(q) 85% phosphoric acid at 440 K
(r) PCC
(s) Bromine water
rows.solution:
The correct matching is I-(r), II-(p), III-(s), IV-(q).

I. OXIDATION OF A PRIMARY ALCOHOL TO AN ALDEHYDE needs PCC, pyridinium chlorochromate. It is a mild oxidising agent in a non-aqueous medium, which is what lets it stop at the aldehyde; a stronger reagent would carry the oxidation on to the carboxylic acid.

II. BUTAN-2-ONE TO BUTAN-2-OL is a REDUCTION of a ketone to a secondary alcohol, and sodium borohydride does it. It is mild enough to leave esters and other groups untouched.

III. BROMINATION OF PHENOL TO THE TRIBROMO PRODUCT needs BROMINE WATER. The aqueous medium lets phenol ionise to phenoxide, which is so strongly activating that all three positions are substituted at once and no catalyst is needed.

IV. DEHYDRATION OF PROPAN-2-OL TO PROPENE needs 85% PHOSPHORIC ACID AT 440 K. The high temperature drives the elimination; the same alcohol at a lower temperature would give an ether instead.

Each reagent is characteristic enough that a single correct pairing fixes the whole answer.

rows.subtopic: Electronic Configurations of the d-Block Elements
rows.stem: The general electronic configuration of d-block elements is :
rows.solution:
The general electronic configuration of the d-block is
\((n-1)d^{1-10}\,ns^{1-2}\)

The \((n-1)d\) subshell is the one being FILLED across the block, so its occupancy must run over the whole range from 1 to 10 — a fixed \(d^{10}\) would describe only the last column, and \(d^0\) would describe no d-block element at all.

The outer \(ns\) subshell holds one or two electrons. Two is the usual case; ONE occurs where an electron has moved into the d set to reach a half-filled or filled subshell, as in chromium, \(3d^5 4s^1\), and copper, \(3d^{10}4s^1\). No d-block element has three \(s\) electrons, since an \(s\) orbital holds at most two.

Note that this formula covers the BLOCK. The definition of a transition ELEMENT is narrower — a partly filled d subshell in the atom or in a stable ion — which is why zinc, cadmium and mercury sit in the block without being transition elements.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : p-nitrophenol is less acidic than phenol.
Reason (R) : Nitro group is electron withdrawing and helps in the stabilisation of p-nitrophenoxide ion.
rows.context: For questions number 13 to 16, two statements are given – one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below :

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
The Assertion is FALSE while the Reason is TRUE.

p-Nitrophenol is MORE acidic than phenol, not less — \(\mathrm{pK_a}\) about 7.1 against 10, nearly a thousandfold difference. The Assertion states the comparison backwards.

The Reason is correct, and it is exactly why the Assertion fails. The nitro group is strongly electron WITHDRAWING, and from the para position it withdraws by resonance as well as inductively — it can take the negative charge of the phenoxide ion right onto its own oxygen. A more stable anion means the proton leaves more readily, so the acid is STRONGER.

So the Reason as written states the case against the Assertion, which is the signature of this answer.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : Benzoic acid does not undergo Friedel – Crafts reaction.
Reason (R) : Carboxyl group is deactivating and the catalyst aluminium chloride gets bonded to the carboxyl group.
rows.context: For questions number 13 to 16, two statements are given – one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below :

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
Both statements are true and the Reason IS the correct explanation of the Assertion.

Benzoic acid genuinely does not undergo Friedel-Crafts reaction, and the Reason names both of the things that stop it.

The carboxyl group is DEACTIVATING: it withdraws electron density from the ring, so the ring is poor at attacking an electrophile — the opposite of what a Friedel-Crafts reaction needs.

And the catalyst, aluminium chloride, is a LEWIS ACID that bonds to the lone pair on the carboxyl oxygen. The catalyst is thereby tied up, and the group it is attached to now withdraws electrons more strongly still.

The same pair of reasons applies to any strongly deactivated ring, which is why Friedel-Crafts reactions fail on nitrobenzene as well.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : Fructose is a reducing sugar.
Reason (R) : Fructose does not reduce Fehling solution and Tollen's reagent.
rows.context: For questions number 13 to 16, two statements are given – one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below :

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE.

Fructose IS a reducing sugar, so the Assertion holds — and that is initially surprising, since fructose is a KETOse and a ketone group is not normally oxidised by a mild reagent.

The Reason simply denies the observation. Fructose DOES reduce both Fehling's solution and Tollens' reagent.

The explanation is that these reagents are ALKALINE. In alkali fructose isomerises to glucose and mannose through an enediol intermediate, and the aldehyde group so exposed is what reduces the reagent. So the test does not detect the ketone directly; it detects what the ketose becomes in the medium.

Any sugar with a free anomeric carbon is reducing, aldose and ketose alike — which is why sucrose, with neither anomeric carbon free, is the one common disaccharide that is not.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : For a Daniell cell, \(\mathrm{Zn/Zn^{2+}}\)(1M) \(||\) \(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}\) (1M)/Cu with \(\mathrm{E^{o}cell}\) = 1.1 V, if the external opposing potential is more than 1.1 V, the electrons flow from Cu to Zn.
Reason (R) : Cell acts like a galvanic cell.
rows.context: For questions number 13 to 16, two statements are given – one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below :

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE.

When an external opposing potential EXCEEDS the cell's own, it overpowers the cell: current is forced through in the opposite direction, the electrode reactions reverse, and electrons flow from copper to zinc. So the Assertion is correct.

But the Reason misnames what the cell is then doing. Under those conditions it is NO LONGER acting as a galvanic cell — it is acting as an ELECTROLYTIC one, with electrical energy being spent to drive a non-spontaneous chemical change rather than chemical energy producing electricity.

The three regimes are worth holding together. While \(E_{\text{ext}} < E_{\text{cell}}\) the cell wins and works galvanically. At \(E_{\text{ext}} = E_{\text{cell}}\) no current flows at all, which is how a cell's potential is measured without drawing current from it. Above that, the cell is being electrolysed — which is exactly how a lead storage battery is recharged.

rows.subtopic: Factors Influencing Rate of a Reaction
rows.stem:
Define the following terms :
(a) Order of a reaction
(b) Activation energy
rows.solution:
(a) ORDER OF A REACTION is the SUM OF THE POWERS to which the concentration terms are raised in the experimentally determined rate law.

For \(\text{Rate} = k[\mathrm{A}]^m[\mathrm{B}]^n\) the order is \(m + n\). It is an EXPERIMENTAL quantity — it cannot be read off the balanced equation — and it may be zero, fractional or a whole number.

(b) ACTIVATION ENERGY is the MINIMUM EXTRA ENERGY that reacting molecules must possess, over and above their average energy, before a collision between them can lead to reaction. Equivalently, it is the energy needed to form the ACTIVATED COMPLEX, the transition state at the top of the energy barrier.

It appears in the Arrhenius equation as \(E_a\), and the fraction of molecules carrying at least that much is \(e^{-E_a/RT}\). A lower barrier means a larger fraction and a faster reaction, which is why a catalyst works by lowering it.

rows.subtopic: Colligative Properties and Determination of Molar Mass
rows.stem: 18 g of a non-volatile solute is dissolved in 200 g of \(\mathrm{H_2O}\) freezes at 272.07 K. Calculate the molecular mass of solute (\(\mathrm{K_f}\) for water = 1.86 \(\mathrm{K\ kg\ mol^{-1}}\))
rows.solution:
The solution freezes at 272.07 K, and pure water at 273.15 K, so the depression is
\(\Delta T_f = 273{\cdot}15 - 272{\cdot}07 = 1{\cdot}08\ \mathrm{K}\)

Combine the freezing point depression formula with the mass data:
\(\Delta T_f = \dfrac{K_f \times w_B \times 1000}{M_B \times w_A}\)

Rearranging for the molar mass, with \(w_B = 18\) g of solute and \(w_A = 200\) g of water:
\(M_B = \dfrac{K_f \times w_B \times 1000}{w_A \times \Delta T_f} = \dfrac{1{\cdot}86 \times 18 \times 1000}{200 \times 1{\cdot}08}\)
\(= \dfrac{33480}{216}\)

\(M_B = 155\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}\)

Note the freezing point of water taken as 273.15 K rather than 273 K. The difference matters here: using 273 would give \(\Delta T_f = 0{\cdot}93\) K and a molar mass of 180, which is a substantially different answer from a change in the third significant figure of an input.

rows.stem:
(a) Which compound in the given pair would undergo \(\mathrm{S_N2}\) reaction at a faster rate and why ?
\(\mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-I}\) and \(\mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-Br}\)
(b) Arrange the following compounds in the increasing order of their boiling points :
Butane, 1–Bromobutane, 1–Iodobutane, 1–Chlorobutane
rows.solution:
(a) IODOETHANE, \(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2I}\), reacts faster.

With the same carbon skeleton in both, the only variable is how good a leaving group the halogen makes. In an \(\mathrm{S_N}2\) reaction the carbon-halogen bond breaks as the nucleophile attacks, so the WEAKER that bond, the faster the reaction.

The \(\mathrm{C-I}\) bond is weaker than the \(\mathrm{C-Br}\) bond, because iodine is the larger atom and its orbital overlaps carbon's less well. The iodide ion is also the more stable of the two anions, being larger and better able to spread its charge — a better leaving group in both senses.

(b) Increasing order of boiling point:
BUTANE < 1-CHLOROBUTANE < 1-BROMOBUTANE < 1-IODOBUTANE

All four have the same carbon skeleton, so the ordering follows the MOLECULAR MASS and, with it, the strength of the van der Waals forces. A larger, more polarisable halogen gives a larger induced dipole and a higher boiling point.

Butane, with no halogen at all, is much the lightest and boils lowest — at 273 K against about 403 K for 1-iodobutane.

rows.subtopic: Chemical Reactions of Aldehydes and Ketones
rows.stem: Write the stepwise mechanism of nucleophilic addition reactions in the carbonyl compounds.
rows.solution:
NUCLEOPHILIC ADDITION to a carbonyl compound proceeds in TWO steps.

Why it happens at all: the carbonyl carbon is electron deficient, because oxygen is more electronegative and pulls the \(\pi\) electrons towards itself, leaving the carbon with a partial POSITIVE charge and the oxygen a partial negative one. A nucleophile is therefore attracted to the carbon.

STEP 1 — attack by the nucleophile. The nucleophile approaches the carbonyl carbon from a direction roughly PERPENDICULAR to the plane of the group, and as the bond forms the \(\pi\) electrons shift entirely onto the oxygen:
\(\mathrm{Nu^-} + \mathrm{C{=}O} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Nu{-}C{-}O^-}\)
The carbon changes from \(sp^2\) to \(sp^3\), so the flat carbonyl group becomes a pyramidal alkoxide ion. This step is SLOW and rate determining.

STEP 2 — protonation. The alkoxide ion picks up a proton from the medium, giving the neutral product:
\(\mathrm{Nu{-}C{-}O^-} + \mathrm{H^+} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Nu{-}C{-}OH}\)
This step is FAST.

Note the contrast with an alkene, whose \(\pi\) bond is electron RICH and therefore attracts electrophiles. The carbonyl group's polarisation is what reverses the kind of reagent it attracts.

rows.subtopic: Methods of Preparation of Carboxylic Acids
rows.stem:
How will you convert the following :
(i) Toluene to benzoic acid.
(ii) Ethanol to 3-Hydroxybutanal
rows.solution:
(i) TOLUENE TO BENZOIC ACID. Alkaline permanganate oxidises the methyl side chain right down to the carboxyl group, and acidification then frees the acid:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5CH_3} \xrightarrow[2.\ \mathrm{H_3O^+}]{1.\ \mathrm{KMnO_4},\ \mathrm{KOH}} \mathrm{C_6H_5COOH}\)
The ring itself is untouched — benzene rings resist oxidation, which is why the attack falls on the side chain.

(ii) ETHANOL TO 3-HYDROXYBUTANAL, in two steps. Count the carbons first: two in, four out, so a COUPLING is needed — and a hydroxyl group beta to an aldehyde is the signature of an ALDOL ADDITION.

Oxidise the ethanol to ethanal with a mild reagent that stops at the aldehyde:
\(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2OH} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{PCC}} \mathrm{CH_3CHO}\)

Then treat with dilute alkali WITHOUT heating, so the addition stops at the \(\beta\)-hydroxy aldehyde:
\(2\mathrm{CH_3CHO} \xrightarrow{\text{dil. }\mathrm{NaOH}} \mathrm{CH_3CH(OH)CH_2CHO}\)

Heating would dehydrate the product to but-2-enal, so the mild condition is essential.

rows.stem:
(a) What happens when glucose reacts with bromine water ? Write chemical equation.
(b) Two bases are mentioned below, identify which is present in DNA and which one is present in RNA :
(i) Thymine, (ii) Uracil.
rows.solution:
(a) Bromine water oxidises glucose to a six carbon carboxylic acid, GLUCONIC ACID:
\(\mathrm{CHO(CHOH)_4CH_2OH} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{Br_2}\text{ water}} \mathrm{COOH(CHOH)_4CH_2OH}\)

Bromine water is a MILD oxidising agent, too mild to attack a hydroxyl group, so the only thing in the molecule it can have oxidised is the ALDEHYDE — and that specificity is what makes the reaction a proof that glucose contains an aldehyde group.

(b) THYMINE is present in DNA; URACIL is present in RNA.

Both nucleic acids carry adenine, guanine and cytosine; only the fourth base differs. Thymine is uracil with a methyl group added, so the two are closely related and pair with adenine in the same way.

rows.stem:
(a) Draw the geometrical isomers of the given complex :
\(\mathrm{[Pt(en)_2Cl_2]^{2+}}\)
(b) Write the electronic configuration for \(\mathrm{d^4}\) ion if \(\Delta_0 < \mathrm{P}\) on the basis of crystal field theory.
(c) What is meant by a unidentate ligand ? Give an example.
rows.solution:
(a) \(\mathrm{[Pt(en)_2Cl_2]^{2+}}\) is octahedral with two chlorido ligands and two bidentate diamines, so the two chlorides may sit adjacent or opposite.

CIS ISOMER: the two chlorido ligands on ADJACENT positions, with the two diamine ligands spanning the remaining four. This form has no plane of symmetry and is therefore also optically active.

TRANS ISOMER: the two chlorido ligands directly OPPOSITE each other along one axis, with the two chelate rings lying in the plane between them. This form has a plane of symmetry and is optically inactive.

(b) \(\Delta_{\mathrm{o}} < \mathrm{P}\) means the splitting costs LESS than pairing, so electrons spread out singly before any pair up. For \(d^4\):
\(t_{2g}^3\,e_g^1\)
with four unpaired electrons — a HIGH SPIN complex. Had \(\Delta_{\mathrm{o}}\) exceeded \(\mathrm{P}\), the configuration would have been \(t_{2g}^4\,e_g^0\), low spin, with two.

(c) A UNIDENTATE ligand is one that binds the metal through a SINGLE donor atom — it has only one site with which to attach, so it occupies one position in the coordination sphere.

Examples: the chloride ion, \(\mathrm{Cl^-}\); water; ammonia.

The contrast is with a BIDENTATE ligand such as ethane-1,2-diamine, which binds through two donor atoms at once and closes a chelate ring.

rows.stem:
Calculate emf of the following cell at \(25\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\) :
\(\mathrm{Sn/Sn^{2+}}\ (0.001\ \mathrm{M})\ ||\ \mathrm{H^+}\ (0.01\ \mathrm{M})\ |\ \mathrm{H_{2(g)}}(1\ \mathrm{bar})\ |\ \mathrm{Pt_{(s)}}\)
Given : \(\mathrm{E^{\circ}(Sn^{2+}/Sn)} = -0.14\) V, \(\mathrm{E^{\circ}\ H^+/H_2} = 0.00\) V (log 10 = 1)
rows.solution:
Read the cell diagram: the ANODE is written on the left, so tin is oxidised and the hydrogen electrode on the right is the cathode.

\(E^{\circ}_{\text{cell}} = E^{\circ}_{\text{cathode}} - E^{\circ}_{\text{anode}} = 0{\cdot}00 - (-0{\cdot}14) = 0{\cdot}14\ \mathrm{V}\)

The cell reaction is \(\mathrm{Sn} + 2\mathrm{H^+} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Sn^{2+}} + \mathrm{H_2}\), so \(n = 2\). Solid tin does not enter the quotient, and hydrogen at 1 bar contributes a factor of 1:
\(E_{\text{cell}} = E^{\circ}_{\text{cell}} - \dfrac{0{\cdot}059}{2}\log\dfrac{[\mathrm{Sn^{2+}}]}{[\mathrm{H^+}]^2}\)
\(= 0{\cdot}14 - \dfrac{0{\cdot}059}{2}\log\dfrac{0{\cdot}001}{(0{\cdot}01)^2}\)
\(= 0{\cdot}14 - 0{\cdot}0295 \times \log 10\)
\(= 0{\cdot}14 - 0{\cdot}0295\)

\(E_{\text{cell}} = 0{\cdot}1105\ \mathrm{V}\), that is about \(0{\cdot}11\) V

Note the SQUARED term in the denominator. \((0{\cdot}01)^2\) is \(10^{-4}\), not \(10^{-2}\), so the quotient is 10 rather than 0.1 — and getting that wrong flips the sign of the correction.

rows.stem:
Write chemical equations for the following reactions : (Do any three)
(a) Hydroboration – oxidation reaction
(b) Williamson Synthesis
(c) Friedel-Crafts Alkylation of Anisole
(d) Reimer-Tiemann Reaction
rows.solution:
(a) HYDROBORATION-OXIDATION adds water across a double bond ANTI-Markovnikov: the hydroxyl goes to the carbon carrying MORE hydrogens, because boron, being the bulkier and less electronegative atom, attaches to the less hindered carbon.
\(\mathrm{CH_3{-}CH{=}CH_2} \xrightarrow[2.\ \mathrm{H_2O_2},\ \mathrm{OH^-}]{1.\ \mathrm{B_2H_6}} \mathrm{CH_3{-}CH_2{-}CH_2{-}OH}\)
Acid-catalysed hydration of the same alkene would give propan-2-ol instead, which is what makes this route worth having.

(b) WILLIAMSON SYNTHESIS makes an ether by letting a sodium alkoxide displace halide from an alkyl halide in a single bimolecular step:
\(\mathrm{R{-}X} + \mathrm{R'{-}ONa} \longrightarrow \mathrm{R{-}O{-}R'} + \mathrm{NaX}\)
Because the step is \(\mathrm{S_N}2\), the HALIDE must be primary; a tertiary halide would eliminate instead. Its value is that it makes UNSYMMETRICAL ethers, which dehydrating an alcohol cannot.

(c) FRIEDEL-CRAFTS ALKYLATION OF ANISOLE. The methoxy group is activating and ORTHO, PARA directing, so a mixture of the two isomers results:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5OCH_3} + \mathrm{CH_3Cl} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{CS_2}]{\text{anhyd. }\mathrm{AlCl_3}} \mathrm{o\text{-}CH_3O{-}C_6H_4{-}CH_3} + \mathrm{p\text{-}CH_3O{-}C_6H_4{-}CH_3}\)

(d) REIMER-TIEMANN REACTION. Chloroform with aqueous alkali generates dichlorocarbene, which attacks the phenoxide ion at its ORTHO position; acidification then frees the aldehyde:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5OH} \xrightarrow[2.\ \mathrm{H^+}]{1.\ \mathrm{CHCl_3} + \text{aq. }\mathrm{NaOH}} \mathrm{o\text{-}HO{-}C_6H_4{-}CHO}\)
The product is salicylaldehyde.

rows.stem:
(a) Give chemical tests to distinguish between the following pairs of compounds :
(i) Phenol and Benzoic acid
(ii) Propanal and Propanone
(b) Which one of the given compounds is a stronger acid and why ?
\(\mathrm{CH_2FCH_2CH_2COOH}\) or \(\mathrm{CH_3CHFCH_2COOH}\)
rows.solution:
(a)(i) PHENOL AND BENZOIC ACID — use NEUTRAL IRON(III) CHLORIDE. Phenol gives a VIOLET colouration, from a coloured iron-phenoxide complex; benzoic acid gives no violet colour.

Sodium hydrogencarbonate distinguishes them the other way round: benzoic acid effervesces, releasing carbon dioxide, while phenol does not — phenol is too weak an acid to displace carbonic acid.

(ii) PROPANAL AND PROPANONE — use TOLLENS' REAGENT. Warm each with ammoniacal silver nitrate: propanal, being an ALDEHYDE, is oxidised and deposits a silver mirror; propanone, a ketone, does not react.

Fehling's solution serves equally well, giving a red precipitate of copper(I) oxide with the aldehyde alone. Note the iodoform test would be no use here — propanone gives it but so does nothing else in the pair, and propanal does not, so it would work, but Tollens' is the direct test for the aldehyde group.

(b) \(\mathrm{CH_3CHFCH_2COOH}\) is the stronger acid.

Both molecules carry the same fluorine on the same four-carbon chain; only its POSITION differs. Fluorine withdraws electron density inductively, which disperses the negative charge on the carboxylate ion and stabilises it — and a more stable anion means a stronger acid.

But the inductive effect is transmitted THROUGH BONDS and falls away sharply with distance. In \(\mathrm{CH_3CHFCH_2COOH}\) the fluorine is on the \(\beta\) carbon, one bond nearer the carboxyl group than in \(\mathrm{CH_2FCH_2CH_2COOH}\), where it sits on the \(\gamma\) carbon.

Nearer means a stronger pull, a better stabilised anion, and the stronger acid.

rows.stem:
Explain the following terms :
(a) Essential amino acids
(b) Peptide bond
(c) Denaturation
rows.solution:
(a) ESSENTIAL AMINO ACIDS are those the body CANNOT synthesise for itself; they have to be supplied in the diet. Valine, leucine, isoleucine and lysine are among them.

The contrast is with NON-ESSENTIAL amino acids, such as glycine and alanine, which the body can make. The name describes what the DIET must supply, not how important the acid is — both kinds are needed for protein synthesis.

(b) A PEPTIDE BOND is the amide linkage \(-\mathrm{CO-NH}-\) that joins two amino acids. The carboxyl group of one condenses with the amino group of the next, a molecule of water is lost, and the bond formed between that carbon and that nitrogen is the peptide bond.

It is what builds a protein from its residues, and the sequence those bonds fix is the protein's primary structure.

(c) DENATURATION is the loss of a protein's BIOLOGICAL ACTIVITY when its native structure is destroyed by a physical change such as heating, or a chemical one such as a change in pH.

The weak forces holding the chain in shape are disrupted, so the helix uncoils and the globule unfolds: the SECONDARY and TERTIARY structures are destroyed while the PRIMARY structure survives intact, since no peptide bond is broken. Coagulation of egg white on boiling is the everyday instance, and it is irreversible.

rows.stem:
(a) Write the IUPAC name of the given compound :
(b) The presence of \(\mathrm{-NO_2}\) group at ortho or para position increases the reactivity of haloarenes towards nucleophilic substitution reactions. Give reason to explain the above statement.
(c) What happens when ethyl chloride is treated with alcoholic potassium hydroxide ?
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED — part (a) prints a DRAWN skeletal structure and asks for its IUPAC name, so the figure IS the question: a six-membered carbocycle with one endocyclic double bond, a halogen label on the ring vertex at the top of that double bond and a second, different halogen label on the ring vertex two positions clockwise from it. It is deliberately NOT named or given as a formula, because naming it would state the answer. Page idx 14.
rows.solution:
(a) The compound is a cyclohexene ring carrying a chlorine on one of its doubly bonded carbons and a bromine on the carbon next to it.

Number the ring so that the double bond gets the lowest locants and the principal chain keeps them low: the chlorine-bearing alkene carbon is \(\mathrm{C_1}\), its partner \(\mathrm{C_2}\), and the bromine-bearing carbon \(\mathrm{C_3}\). Substituents are then cited alphabetically, bromo before chloro:
3-BROMO-1-CHLOROCYCLOHEXENE

Note that the two halogens are in quite different environments — the chlorine is VINYLIC, on an \(sp^2\) carbon, and the bromine ALLYLIC, on the \(sp^3\) carbon beside the double bond. That difference makes the bromine enormously the more reactive of the two.

(b) Because a nitro group at the ORTHO or PARA position STABILISES THE INTERMEDIATE CARBANION.

Nucleophilic substitution on a haloarene goes through a negatively charged intermediate, formed when the nucleophile adds to the ring carbon holding the halogen. The more stable that intermediate, the lower the energy barrier and the faster the reaction.

A nitro group is strongly electron withdrawing, and from the ortho or para position it can accept that negative charge RIGHT ONTO ITS OWN OXYGEN by resonance. It also pulls electron density out of the ring generally, which makes the ring less repellent to the approaching nucleophile.

The POSITION is essential: a nitro group at the META position cannot accept the charge by resonance and has almost no effect.

(c) ELIMINATION occurs and ETHENE is formed.

Alcoholic potassium hydroxide supplies ALKOXIDE ions, which are much stronger BASES than hydroxide but bulkier and poorer nucleophiles. An alkoxide therefore attacks a \(\beta\) HYDROGEN rather than the carbon, and the chloride leaves along with it:
\(\mathrm{CH_3{-}CH_2{-}Cl} + \mathrm{KOH(alc.)} \longrightarrow \mathrm{CH_2{=}CH_2} + \mathrm{KCl} + \mathrm{H_2O}\)

AQUEOUS potassium hydroxide would have given ethanol instead, by substitution. Substitution and elimination are always in competition; what the solvent changes is which one wins.

rows.stem: Show that the time required for 99.9% completion in a first order reaction is 10 times of half-life (\(\mathrm{t_{1/2}}\)) of the reaction [log 2 = 0.3010, log 10 = 1].
rows.solution:
Take the first order integrated rate equation and apply it twice, to the two completions asked about.

FOR 99.9% COMPLETION. Let \([\mathrm{R}]_0 = 100\); then 99.9 has reacted and \([\mathrm{R}] = 0{\cdot}1\):
\(t_{99{\cdot}9\%} = \dfrac{2{\cdot}303}{k}\log\dfrac{100}{0{\cdot}1} = \dfrac{2{\cdot}303}{k}\log 1000 = \dfrac{2{\cdot}303}{k} \times 3\)   ... (i)

FOR 50% COMPLETION — the half-life. Let \([\mathrm{R}]_0 = 100\); then \([\mathrm{R}] = 50\):
\(t_{1/2} = \dfrac{2{\cdot}303}{k}\log\dfrac{100}{50} = \dfrac{2{\cdot}303}{k}\log 2 = \dfrac{2{\cdot}303}{k} \times 0{\cdot}3010\)   ... (ii)

DIVIDE (i) BY (ii). Everything but the logarithms cancels — the rate constant along with the rest:
\(\dfrac{t_{99{\cdot}9\%}}{t_{1/2}} = \dfrac{3}{0{\cdot}3010} = 10\)

so \(t_{99{\cdot}9\%} = 10 \times t_{1/2}\), as required.

The cancellation of \(k\) is what makes the result general: it holds for EVERY first order reaction, fast or slow, which is why it can be stated as a bare ratio with no numbers attached.

rows.stem:
Predict whether \(\mathrm{[CoF_6]^{3-}}\) is diamagnetic or paramagnetic and why ?
[Atomic number : Co = 27]
rows.context: The nature of bonding, structure of the coordination compound can be explained to some extent by valence bond theory. The central metal atom/ion makes available a number of vacant orbitals equal to its coordination number. The appropriate atomic orbitals (s, p and d) of the metal hybridise to give a set of equivalent orbitals of definite geometry such as square planar, tetrahedral, octahedral and so on. A strong covalent bond is formed only when the orbitals overlap to the maximum extent. The d-orbitals involved in the hybridisation may be either inner d-orbitals i.e. (n–1) d or outer d-orbitals i.e. nd. The complexes formed are called inner orbital complex (low spin complex) and outer orbital complex (high spin complex) respectively. Further, the complexes can be paramagnetic or diamagnetic in nature. The drawbacks of this theory are that this involves number of assumptions and also does not explain the colour of the complex.
rows.solution:
\(\mathrm{[CoF_6]^{3-}}\) is PARAMAGNETIC.

Cobalt is atomic number 27, so the neutral atom is \([\mathrm{Ar}]\,3d^7 4s^2\). Six fluorides give \(-6\) against an overall \(-3\), so cobalt is \(+3\) and \(\mathrm{Co^{3+}}\) is \(3d^6\).

Fluoride is a WEAK FIELD ligand: the splitting it produces is smaller than the pairing energy, so it CANNOT force the electrons to pair. The six electrons therefore spread out as far as they can — \(t_{2g}^4\,e_g^2\) — leaving FOUR UNPAIRED.

Unpaired electrons mean paramagnetism, with \(\mu = \sqrt{4(4+2)} = 4{\cdot}90\) B.M.

The contrast is \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_6]^{3+}}\), where ammonia is a strong enough field ligand to pair all six into \(t_{2g}^6\) — that complex is diamagnetic, from the very same \(3d^6\) ion.

rows.subtopic: Definitions of Some Important Terms Pertaining to Coordination Compounds
rows.stem: What is the coordination number of Co in \(\mathrm{[Co(en)_2\ Cl_2]^{+}}\) ?
rows.context: The nature of bonding, structure of the coordination compound can be explained to some extent by valence bond theory. The central metal atom/ion makes available a number of vacant orbitals equal to its coordination number. The appropriate atomic orbitals (s, p and d) of the metal hybridise to give a set of equivalent orbitals of definite geometry such as square planar, tetrahedral, octahedral and so on. A strong covalent bond is formed only when the orbitals overlap to the maximum extent. The d-orbitals involved in the hybridisation may be either inner d-orbitals i.e. (n–1) d or outer d-orbitals i.e. nd. The complexes formed are called inner orbital complex (low spin complex) and outer orbital complex (high spin complex) respectively. Further, the complexes can be paramagnetic or diamagnetic in nature. The drawbacks of this theory are that this involves number of assumptions and also does not explain the colour of the complex.
rows.solution:
The coordination number of cobalt is SIX.

Coordination number counts DONOR ATOMS attached to the metal, not ligand molecules. Ethane-1,2-diamine is BIDENTATE: it binds through both of its nitrogens at once, closing a five-membered chelate ring.

Two such ligands supply \(2 \times 2 = 4\) donor atoms, and the two chlorido ligands supply one each — a total of SIX, and the complex is octahedral.

Counting the four LIGANDS instead of the six donor atoms gives 4, which is the answer the question is testing for.

rows.stem:
(i) Write the IUPAC name of the given complex :
\(\mathrm{[Pt(NH_3)_2Cl_2]^{2+}}\)
(ii) Explain \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_6]^{3+}}\) is an inner orbital or outer orbital complex.
rows.context: The nature of bonding, structure of the coordination compound can be explained to some extent by valence bond theory. The central metal atom/ion makes available a number of vacant orbitals equal to its coordination number. The appropriate atomic orbitals (s, p and d) of the metal hybridise to give a set of equivalent orbitals of definite geometry such as square planar, tetrahedral, octahedral and so on. A strong covalent bond is formed only when the orbitals overlap to the maximum extent. The d-orbitals involved in the hybridisation may be either inner d-orbitals i.e. (n–1) d or outer d-orbitals i.e. nd. The complexes formed are called inner orbital complex (low spin complex) and outer orbital complex (high spin complex) respectively. Further, the complexes can be paramagnetic or diamagnetic in nature. The drawbacks of this theory are that this involves number of assumptions and also does not explain the colour of the complex.
rows.solution:
(i) Two ammonia molecules are neutral and two chlorido ligands give \(-2\), so against an overall charge of \(+2\) platinum must be \(+4\).

Ligands are named alphabetically, ammine before chlorido, and the complex is a cation, so the metal keeps its ordinary name:
DIAMMINEDICHLORIDOPLATINUM(IV) ION

(ii) \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_6]^{3+}}\) is an INNER ORBITAL complex.

Cobalt is \(+3\) here, so \(\mathrm{Co^{3+}}\) is \(3d^6\). Ammonia is a STRONG FIELD ligand, and it forces those six electrons to pair up into the three lower \(3d\) orbitals — \(t_{2g}^6\).

That pairing FREES two INNER \(3d\) orbitals, and bonding uses them together with the \(4s\) and the three \(4p\): hybridisation \(d^2sp^3\). Because the d orbitals used belong to the inner \((n-1)d\) shell, the complex is called an INNER ORBITAL, or low spin, complex — and with every electron paired it is diamagnetic.

Had the ligand been weak, as fluoride is, no pairing would have occurred, no inner orbital would have been free, and bonding would have had to reach outwards to the \(4d\) set instead.

rows.stem: Using valence bond theory, deduce the shape and hybridisation of \(\mathrm{[Ni(NH_3)_6]^{2+}}\) [Atomic number of Ni = 28]
rows.context: The nature of bonding, structure of the coordination compound can be explained to some extent by valence bond theory. The central metal atom/ion makes available a number of vacant orbitals equal to its coordination number. The appropriate atomic orbitals (s, p and d) of the metal hybridise to give a set of equivalent orbitals of definite geometry such as square planar, tetrahedral, octahedral and so on. A strong covalent bond is formed only when the orbitals overlap to the maximum extent. The d-orbitals involved in the hybridisation may be either inner d-orbitals i.e. (n–1) d or outer d-orbitals i.e. nd. The complexes formed are called inner orbital complex (low spin complex) and outer orbital complex (high spin complex) respectively. Further, the complexes can be paramagnetic or diamagnetic in nature. The drawbacks of this theory are that this involves number of assumptions and also does not explain the colour of the complex.
rows.solution:
Nickel is atomic number 28, so the neutral atom is \([\mathrm{Ar}]\,3d^8 4s^2\). The six ammonia molecules are neutral, so against an overall \(+2\) nickel is \(+2\), and \(\mathrm{Ni^{2+}}\) is \(3d^8\).

Eight electrons in five d orbitals must occupy them as three pairs and two singles — \(3d^8\) leaves TWO UNPAIRED whatever the ligand does, because there are simply not enough vacancies to pair them further. No inner \(3d\) orbital can therefore be freed.

Bonding must reach OUTWARDS: it uses the \(4s\), the three \(4p\) and two of the \(4d\) orbitals.

HYBRIDISATION: \(sp^3d^2\)
SHAPE: OCTAHEDRAL

The complex is an OUTER ORBITAL one, high spin, and PARAMAGNETIC with two unpaired electrons, \(\mu = \sqrt{2(2+2)} = 2{\cdot}83\) B.M.

Note that \(d^8\) is the one configuration where the field strength cannot change the count in an octahedral complex — which is why ammonia, an otherwise strong field ligand, gives an outer orbital complex here.

rows.stem: What is the function of a salt bridge in a galvanic cell ?
rows.context: In a galvanic cell, chemical energy of a redox reaction is converted into electrical energy, whereas in an electrolytic cell the redox reaction occurs on passing electricity. The simplest galvanic cell is in which Zn rod is placed in a solution of \(\mathrm{ZnSO_4}\) and Cu rod is placed in a solution of \(\mathrm{CuSO_4}\). The two rods are connected by a metallic wire through a voltmeter. The two solutions are joined by a salt bridge. The difference between the two electrode potentials of the two electrodes is known as electromotive force. In the process of electrolysis, the decomposition of a substance takes place by passing an electric current. One mole of electric charge when passed through a cell will discharge half a mole of a divalent metal ion such as \(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}\). This was first formulated by Faraday in the form of laws of electrolysis.
rows.solution:
A SALT BRIDGE does two things, and they are two sides of the same requirement.

It COMPLETES THE CIRCUIT by allowing ions to flow between the two half-cells, so that current can pass through the solution as well as through the external wire.

And it MAINTAINS ELECTRICAL NEUTRALITY in each half-cell. As the cell runs, positive ions accumulate in the anode compartment while the cathode compartment loses them; without the bridge, charge would build up within seconds and stop the reaction. The bridge lets its own ions migrate to cancel that build-up — anions towards the anode, cations towards the cathode.

It also prevents the two solutions from mixing directly, which would let the reaction occur without generating any current at all.

rows.stem: When does galvanic cell behave like an electrolytic cell ?
rows.context: In a galvanic cell, chemical energy of a redox reaction is converted into electrical energy, whereas in an electrolytic cell the redox reaction occurs on passing electricity. The simplest galvanic cell is in which Zn rod is placed in a solution of \(\mathrm{ZnSO_4}\) and Cu rod is placed in a solution of \(\mathrm{CuSO_4}\). The two rods are connected by a metallic wire through a voltmeter. The two solutions are joined by a salt bridge. The difference between the two electrode potentials of the two electrodes is known as electromotive force. In the process of electrolysis, the decomposition of a substance takes place by passing an electric current. One mole of electric charge when passed through a cell will discharge half a mole of a divalent metal ion such as \(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}\). This was first formulated by Faraday in the form of laws of electrolysis.
rows.solution:
When the EXTERNAL OPPOSING POTENTIAL EXCEEDS the cell's own potential, that is when \(E_{\text{ext}} > E_{\text{cell}}\).

Below that point the cell still wins: while \(E_{\text{ext}} < E_{\text{cell}}\) the reaction continues in its spontaneous direction and the cell works galvanically. At \(E_{\text{ext}} = E_{\text{cell}}\) the current stops altogether and the cell is at equilibrium — which is how a cell's potential is measured without drawing current from it.

Once the external voltage exceeds it, the cell is overpowered: current is forced through in the opposite direction, the electrode reactions reverse, and electrical energy is now being SPENT to drive a non-spontaneous chemical change. That is what an electrolytic cell does, and it is how a lead storage battery is recharged.

rows.stem:
Can copper sulphate solution be stored in a pot made of zinc ? Explain with the help of the value of \(\mathrm{E^{\circ}}\) cell.
(\(\mathrm{E^{\circ}\ Cu^{2+}/Cu}\) = 0.34 V)
(\(\mathrm{E^{\circ}\ Zn^{2+}/Zn}\) = – 0.76 V)
rows.context: In a galvanic cell, chemical energy of a redox reaction is converted into electrical energy, whereas in an electrolytic cell the redox reaction occurs on passing electricity. The simplest galvanic cell is in which Zn rod is placed in a solution of \(\mathrm{ZnSO_4}\) and Cu rod is placed in a solution of \(\mathrm{CuSO_4}\). The two rods are connected by a metallic wire through a voltmeter. The two solutions are joined by a salt bridge. The difference between the two electrode potentials of the two electrodes is known as electromotive force. In the process of electrolysis, the decomposition of a substance takes place by passing an electric current. One mole of electric charge when passed through a cell will discharge half a mole of a divalent metal ion such as \(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}\). This was first formulated by Faraday in the form of laws of electrolysis.
rows.solution:
NO, copper sulphate solution CANNOT be stored in a zinc pot.

Set up the cell that the storage would amount to. Zinc has the more negative potential, so it would be the anode and copper deposited at the cathode:
\(E^{\circ}_{\text{cell}} = E^{\circ}_{\mathrm{Cu^{2+}/Cu}} - E^{\circ}_{\mathrm{Zn^{2+}/Zn}} = 0{\cdot}34 - (-0{\cdot}76)\)

\(E^{\circ}_{\text{cell}} = +1{\cdot}10\ \mathrm{V}\)

A POSITIVE cell potential means a NEGATIVE \(\Delta G\), so the reaction is SPONTANEOUS:
\(\mathrm{Zn(s)} + \mathrm{Cu^{2+}(aq)} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Zn^{2+}(aq)} + \mathrm{Cu(s)}\)

The zinc of the pot would dissolve while copper deposited on it, destroying both the vessel and the solution. Zinc is above copper in the electrochemical series, and any metal above another displaces it from solution.

rows.stem:
How much charge in terms of Faraday is required for the following :
(i) 1 mol of \(\mathrm{MnO_4^-}\) to \(\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}\)
(ii) 1 mol of \(\mathrm{H_2O}\) to \(\mathrm{O_2}\)
rows.context: In a galvanic cell, chemical energy of a redox reaction is converted into electrical energy, whereas in an electrolytic cell the redox reaction occurs on passing electricity. The simplest galvanic cell is in which Zn rod is placed in a solution of \(\mathrm{ZnSO_4}\) and Cu rod is placed in a solution of \(\mathrm{CuSO_4}\). The two rods are connected by a metallic wire through a voltmeter. The two solutions are joined by a salt bridge. The difference between the two electrode potentials of the two electrodes is known as electromotive force. In the process of electrolysis, the decomposition of a substance takes place by passing an electric current. One mole of electric charge when passed through a cell will discharge half a mole of a divalent metal ion such as \(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}\). This was first formulated by Faraday in the form of laws of electrolysis.
rows.solution:
(i) In \(\mathrm{MnO_4^-}\) the four oxides give \(-8\) against an overall \(-1\), so manganese is \(+7\); in \(\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}\) it is \(+2\). Each manganese therefore gains FIVE electrons:
\(\mathrm{MnO_4^-} + 8\mathrm{H^+} + 5e^- \longrightarrow \mathrm{Mn^{2+}} + 4\mathrm{H_2O}\)

One mole of permanganate needs 5 mol of electrons, that is 5 FARADAY.

(ii) Write the half reaction and count electrons PER MOLECULE OF WATER:
\(2\mathrm{H_2O} \longrightarrow \mathrm{O_2} + 4\mathrm{H^+} + 4e^-\)

Four electrons are released for every TWO molecules of water, so ONE mole of water requires 2 mol of electrons, that is 2 FARADAY.

Reading four electrons straight off the equation and answering 4 F is the trap: that figure belongs to 2 mol of water, or equivalently to 1 mol of oxygen.

rows.subtopic: General Properties of the Transition Elements (d-Block)
rows.stem:
Attempt any five of the following :
(a) Why Zinc is not regarded as a transition element ?
(b) What is Lanthanoid contraction ?
(c) Why is first ionization enthalpy of chromium lower than that of Zn ?
(d) Why are transition elements good catalysts ?
(e) Compounds of transition metals are generally coloured. Give reason.
(f) Out of \(\mathrm{KMnO_4}\) and \(\mathrm{K_2MnO_4}\), which one is paramagnetic and why ?
(g) Complete the following ionic equation :
\(\mathrm{Cr_2O_7^{2-}} + 14\,\mathrm{H^+} + 6\mathrm{e^-} \longrightarrow\)
rows.solution:
(a) Because ZINC HAS A COMPLETELY FILLED d SUBSHELL both in the ground state and in its only stable oxidation state.

Zinc is \([\mathrm{Ar}]\,3d^{10}4s^2\) as the atom and \(3d^{10}\) as the \(\mathrm{Zn^{2+}}\) ion. A transition element is DEFINED as one with a PARTLY filled d subshell in the atom or in at least one stable ion, and zinc has no such state. Its compounds are accordingly white, diamagnetic and confined to \(+2\).

(b) LANTHANOID CONTRACTION is the steady DECREASE in atomic and ionic radii across the lanthanoid series, from lanthanum to lutetium, as the atomic number increases.

The cause is poor shielding: each added electron enters a \(4f\) orbital, and \(4f\) orbitals screen the nuclear charge badly, so each added proton pulls the outer electrons in a little harder than the added electron pushes them out.

(c) Because the electron removed comes from a DIFFERENT KIND OF ORBITAL in each case.

Chromium is \(3d^5 4s^1\): its single, loosely held \(4s\) electron is easily removed, and doing so leaves the stable half-filled \(3d^5\) behind. Zinc is \(3d^{10}4s^2\): its \(4s\) orbital is FULL and shielded by a completed d subshell, so its electron is held much more tightly, and removing it breaks up a stable arrangement rather than producing one.

Measured: about 653 kJ per mole for chromium against 906 for zinc.

(d) Because of their VARIABLE OXIDATION STATES and their ability to form COMPLEXES, together with the large SURFACE AREA a finely divided metal provides.

Moving between oxidation states lets a transition metal accept electrons from one reactant and pass them to another, returning to its original state at the end — vanadium(V) oxide in the Contact process works this way. Vacant d orbitals also let it ADSORB reactants onto its surface, holding them close together and weakening their bonds, as iron does in the Haber process.

(e) Because of d-d TRANSITIONS of electrons within the partly filled d orbitals.

Ligands split the five degenerate d orbitals into two sets, and an electron can absorb a photon of visible light and jump from the lower set to the upper. The light absorbed is missing from what passes through, so the compound shows the COMPLEMENTARY colour.

An ion with an empty or completely filled d subshell — \(\mathrm{Sc^{3+}}\) or \(\mathrm{Zn^{2+}}\) — has no such transition available and its compounds are white.

(f) POTASSIUM MANGANATE, \(\mathrm{K_2MnO_4}\), is the paramagnetic one.

Work out the oxidation state in each. In \(\mathrm{K_2MnO_4}\) the two potassiums give \(+2\) and four oxides \(-8\), so manganese is \(+6\) and the ion is \(3d^1\) — ONE unpaired electron, hence paramagnetic. In \(\mathrm{KMnO_4}\) manganese is \(+7\) and the ion is \(3d^0\) — no d electron at all, so nothing to be unpaired, and it is diamagnetic.

The intense colour of permanganate is therefore NOT a d-d transition; it comes from charge transfer, oxygen to metal.

(g) Dichromate is reduced to chromium(III) in acid, each chromium taking three electrons:
\(\mathrm{Cr_2O_7^{2-}} + 14\mathrm{H^+} + 6e^- \longrightarrow 2\mathrm{Cr^{3+}} + 7\mathrm{H_2O}\)

Check the balance: chromium 2 both sides; oxygen 7 on the left against 7 in the water; hydrogen 14 both sides; charge \(-2 + 14 - 6 = +6\) on the left against \(2 \times (+3) = +6\) on the right.

rows.stem:
(i) Define reverse osmosis.
(ii) Why are aquatic species more comfortable in cold water in comparison to warm water ?
(iii) A solution containing 2 g of glucose (M = 180 g \(\mathrm{mol^{-1}}\)) in 100 g of water is prepared at 303 K. If the vapour pressure of pure water at 303 K is 32.8 mm Hg, what would be the vapour pressure of the solution ?
rows.solution:
(i) REVERSE OSMOSIS is what happens when a pressure GREATER THAN THE OSMOTIC PRESSURE is applied to the solution side of a semipermeable membrane.

Ordinary osmosis drives solvent INTO the solution; applying more than enough pressure to stop that reverses the flow, and pure SOLVENT is squeezed OUT of the solution through the membrane.

Its great application is the desalination of sea water: pressure applied to sea water on one side of a suitable membrane forces pure water through, leaving the salt behind.

(ii) Because the SOLUBILITY OF OXYGEN IN WATER FALLS AS THE TEMPERATURE RISES.

Dissolving a gas is an exothermic process, so by Le Chatelier's principle warming drives it backwards. Cold water therefore holds more dissolved oxygen than warm water at the same pressure, and aquatic species, which breathe what is dissolved, are the better off for it.

This is why thermal pollution — warm water discharged from a power station into a river — threatens fish without adding anything toxic at all.

(iii) For a non-volatile solute the relative lowering of vapour pressure equals the mole fraction of the solute, and for a dilute solution that may be taken as the mole RATIO:
\(\dfrac{p_1^{\,\circ} - p_1}{p_1^{\,\circ}} = \dfrac{w_2 \times M_1}{M_2 \times w_1}\)

Substituting — 2 g of glucose of molar mass 180 in 100 g of water of molar mass 18:
\(\dfrac{32{\cdot}8 - p_1}{32{\cdot}8} = \dfrac{2 \times 18}{180 \times 100} = \dfrac{36}{18000} = 0{\cdot}002\)
\(32{\cdot}8 - p_1 = 32{\cdot}8 \times 0{\cdot}002 = 0{\cdot}0656\)

\(p_1 = 32{\cdot}734\ \mathrm{mm\ Hg}\)

Note how small the lowering is — 0.066 mm Hg out of 32.8, a fifth of one per cent — which is what makes this measurement demanding in practice.

rows.stem:
(i) Predict whether Van't Hoff factor will be less or greater than one, when Ethanoic acid is dissolved in benzene.
(ii) Define ideal solution.
(iii) Calculate the mass of \(\mathrm{CaCl_2}\) (molar mass = 111 g \(\mathrm{mol^{-1}}\)) to be dissolved in 500 g of water to lower its freezing point by 2K, assuming that \(\mathrm{CaCl_2}\) undergoes complete dissociation.
(\(\mathrm{K_f}\) for water = 1.86 K kg \(\mathrm{mol^{-1}}\))
rows.solution:
(i) The van't Hoff factor will be LESS THAN ONE.

Ethanoic acid DIMERISES in benzene: two molecules join through a pair of hydrogen bonds, each one's \(\mathrm{O-H}\) reaching the other's carbonyl oxygen. Benzene is non-polar and cannot compete for those hydrogen bonds, so the dimer survives.

The van't Hoff factor is the ratio of the number of particles ACTUALLY present to the number expected from the formula. Association REDUCES the count, so the ratio falls below 1 — and the observed depression in freezing point is correspondingly SMALLER than the formula predicts.

Dissociation would do the opposite and give \(i > 1\).

(ii) An IDEAL SOLUTION is one that obeys RAOULT'S LAW over the ENTIRE RANGE OF CONCENTRATION, for every component.

Two further properties follow and are usually quoted with the definition: \(\Delta_{\text{mix}}H = 0\) and \(\Delta_{\text{mix}}V = 0\). All three hold because the A-B interactions in such a solution are the SAME in strength as the A-A and B-B interactions, so a molecule barely notices which neighbour it has. Benzene with toluene, and n-hexane with n-heptane, are the standard examples.

(iii) Calcium chloride dissociates completely into THREE ions, so \(i = 3\).

Combine the freezing point depression formula with the mass data:
\(\Delta T_f = \dfrac{i \times K_f \times w_B \times 1000}{M_B \times w_A}\)
\(2 = \dfrac{3 \times 1{\cdot}86 \times w_B \times 1000}{111 \times 500}\)

Rearranging for the mass:
\(w_B = \dfrac{2 \times 111 \times 500}{3 \times 1{\cdot}86 \times 1000} = \dfrac{111000}{5580}\)

\(w_B = 19{\cdot}89\ \mathrm{g}\)

The factor of 3 is the whole point. Omitting it would give about 59.7 g — three times too much — because a colligative property counts PARTICLES, and one formula unit of calcium chloride supplies three of them.

rows.stem: An amide 'A' with molecular formula \(\mathrm{C_7H_7ON}\) undergoes Hoffmann Bromamide degradation reaction to give amine 'B'. B' on treatment with nitrous acid at 273-278 K form 'C' and on treatment with chloroform and ethanolic potassium hydroxide forms 'D'. 'C' on treatment, with ethanol gives 'E'. Identify 'A', 'B', 'C' 'D' and 'E.' and write the sequence of chemical equations.
rows.solution:
Work forwards from the formula, which fixes \(\mathrm{A}\) almost by itself.

\(\mathrm{A}\) is \(\mathrm{C_7H_7ON}\) and is an AMIDE that undergoes Hofmann bromamide degradation. Seven carbons with one oxygen and one nitrogen, in a molecule that survives this chemistry, points to the aromatic amide:
\(\mathrm{A} = \mathrm{C_6H_5CONH_2}\), benzamide

Hofmann bromamide degradation converts an amide to a primary amine with ONE CARBON FEWER, so the seven-carbon amide gives a six-carbon amine:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5CONH_2} + \mathrm{Br_2} + 4\mathrm{NaOH} \longrightarrow \mathrm{C_6H_5NH_2} + \mathrm{Na_2CO_3} + 2\mathrm{NaBr} + 2\mathrm{H_2O}\)
\(\mathrm{B} = \mathrm{C_6H_5NH_2}\), aniline

Nitrous acid at 273-278 K diazotises it, and the salt SURVIVES at that temperature because the ring delocalises the positive charge:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5NH_2} \xrightarrow[273\text{-}278\ \mathrm{K}]{\mathrm{NaNO_2}/\mathrm{HCl}} \mathrm{C_6H_5N_2^+Cl^-}\)
\(\mathrm{C} = \mathrm{C_6H_5N_2^+Cl^-}\), benzenediazonium chloride

Chloroform with alcoholic potassium hydroxide is the CARBYLAMINE reaction, which works on \(\mathrm{B}\) because it is a primary amine:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5NH_2} + \mathrm{CHCl_3} + 3\mathrm{KOH} \xrightarrow{\Delta} \mathrm{C_6H_5NC} + 3\mathrm{KCl} + 3\mathrm{H_2O}\)
\(\mathrm{D} = \mathrm{C_6H_5NC}\), phenyl isocyanide

Ethanol reduces the diazonium group, replacing it by hydrogen and being itself oxidised to ethanal:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5N_2^+Cl^-} + \mathrm{C_2H_5OH} \longrightarrow \mathrm{C_6H_6} + \mathrm{N_2} + \mathrm{CH_3CHO} + \mathrm{HCl}\)
\(\mathrm{E} = \mathrm{C_6H_6}\), benzene

Note that \(\mathrm{C}\) and \(\mathrm{D}\) are made from \(\mathrm{B}\) by two DIFFERENT routes, not in sequence — the question branches at the amine.

rows.stem:
(i) (1) What is Hinsberg's reagent ?
(2) Arrange the following compounds in the increasing order of their basic strength in gaseous phase :
\(\mathrm{C_2H_5NH_2}\), \(\mathrm{(C_2H_5)_3\,N}\), \(\mathrm{(C_2H_5)_2\,NH}\)
(ii) Give reasons for the following :
(1) Methyl amine is more basic than aniline.
(2) Aniline readily reacts with bromine water to give 2, 4, 6-tribromoaniline.
(3) Primary amines have higher boiling points than tertiary amines.
rows.solution:
(i)(1) HINSBERG'S REAGENT is BENZENESULPHONYL CHLORIDE, \(\mathrm{C_6H_5SO_2Cl}\).

It separates the three classes of amine because each responds differently. A primary amine gives a sulphonamide that keeps one acidic hydrogen on nitrogen, so its product dissolves in alkali; a secondary amine gives one with no hydrogen left, so its product is insoluble in alkali; and a tertiary amine, having no nitrogen-hydrogen bond at all, does not react.

(2) Increasing basic strength in the GAS PHASE:
\(\mathrm{C_2H_5NH_2} < (\mathrm{C_2H_5})_2\mathrm{NH} < (\mathrm{C_2H_5})_3\mathrm{N}\)

In the gas phase there is no solvent, so no cation needs to be stabilised by hydrogen bonding and no alkyl group gets in the way of water. Only the INDUCTIVE effect operates: each ethyl group RELEASES electron density onto the nitrogen, making the lone pair more available, so basicity rises steadily with the number of them.

The qualification "in gaseous phase" is load-bearing. In AQUEOUS solution solvation matters too, and the order becomes tertiary, primary, secondary — with the tertiary amine LAST rather than first.

(ii)(1) Because in ANILINE the nitrogen's lone pair is DELOCALISED INTO THE RING by resonance, so it is less available to accept a proton. The nitrogen is also attached to an \(sp^2\) carbon, which is more electronegative and pulls density away from it.

In METHYLAMINE there is no ring to absorb the lone pair, and the methyl group RELEASES electron density towards the nitrogen, making that pair still more available. The difference is large — \(\mathrm{pK_b}\) about 3.4 against aniline's 9.4.

(2) Because the AMINO GROUP IS SO STRONGLY ACTIVATING.

Its lone pair is fed into the ring by resonance, raising the electron density most at the ortho and para positions. The ring is then reactive enough to attack even the feeble electrophile present in bromine water, and all three of those positions are substituted at once — no catalyst is needed, and the white precipitate appears immediately.

Stopping at a monobromo product requires the amino group to be MODERATED first, by acetylating it.

(3) Because PRIMARY AMINES FORM MORE EXTENSIVE INTERMOLECULAR HYDROGEN BONDS.

A primary amine has TWO hydrogens on its nitrogen, so its molecules associate strongly with one another. A tertiary amine has NONE at all — every position is taken by a carbon group — so its molecules cannot hydrogen bond to each other and are held only by weak dipole-dipole forces.

More hydrogen bonding means more energy needed to separate the molecules, so the primary amine boils higher. A secondary amine, with one such hydrogen, falls between the two.
